butir.teks: If that does not occur to him and he dies before believing that the speech of Allah, glorified is He, is eternal, that He can be seen, that He is not a locus for originated events, and so on from what is mentioned among the articles of belief, he has died as a Muslim by consensus (ijma'). But these thoughts that give rise to beliefs: some occur by nature, and some occur through hearing from the people of the town. So if he is in a town where theology (kalam) has spread and people speak of innovations, he should be protected from them at the start of his maturity by being taught the truth, for if falsehood were cast to him, removing it from his heart would become obligatory, and that might be difficult, just as, if this Muslim were a merchant and dealing in usury had spread in the town, it would be obligatory for him to learn to guard against usury. This is the truth regarding the knowledge that is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn), and its meaning is the knowledge of how to perform the obligatory act. Whoever knows the obligatory knowledge and the time of its becoming obligatory has known the knowledge that is an individual obligation. And what the Sufis mention of understanding the promptings of the enemy and the inspiration of the angel is also true, but with respect to the one who sets himself to it. Since the usual case is that a person is not free of the incitements of evil, showing off (riya'), and envy, he must learn from the knowledge of the quarter of destructive traits what he sees himself in need of. How could it not be obligatory for him, when the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "Three things are destructive: obeyed miserliness, followed caprice, and a person's self-admiration" (١) and no human being is free of them. The rest of the blameworthy states of the heart that we will mention, such as arrogance, self-admiration, and their sisters, follow these three destructive things, and removing them is an individual obligation, and it is not possible to remove them except by knowing their limits, knowing their causes, knowing their signs, and knowing their remedy, for whoever does not know evil falls into it, and the remedy is to oppose the cause with its opposite, and how could that be possible without knowing the cause and the thing caused? Most of what we mentioned in the quarter of destructive traits belongs to the individual obligations, and people, all of them, have left them, busying themselves with what does not concern them.

Among what should not be hastened in casting to him, if he has not moved from one religion to another, is belief in Paradise and the Fire, the gathering and the resurrection, until he believes in it and affirms it. It is part of the completion of the two testimonies of faith, for after affirming that he (peace be upon him) is a messenger,

he should understand the message that he conveys, namely that whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger has Paradise, and whoever disobeys them has the Fire. So when you are alert to this gradation, you will know that this is the true position, and you will be certain that every servant, in the course of his states in his day and night, is not free of occurrences in his worship and dealings, with newly arising obligations upon him; so he must ask about everything of rare cases that befalls him, and must hasten to learn what is most likely to occur soon. When it is clear that he (peace and blessings be upon him) meant, by the knowledge made definite with alif and lam in his saying (peace and blessings be upon him), "Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim," only the knowledge of action that is well known to be obligatory upon Muslims, and nothing else, then the aspect of the gradation and the time of its becoming obligatory are clear. And Allah knows best.
Chapter Three: On what the common people consider among the praiseworthy sciences, though it is not among them

In it: an explanation of the aspect by which some sciences may be blameworthy; an explanation of the changing of the names of the sciences, namely jurisprudence (fiqh), knowledge, affirmation of Divine oneness (tawhid), admonition, and wisdom; and an explanation of the praiseworthy measure of the religious sciences and the blameworthy measure of them.

Explanation of the reason for the blame of blameworthy knowledge. Perhaps you will say: Knowledge is knowing a thing as it is, and it is among the attributes of Allah Most High; so how can a thing be knowledge and, despite being knowledge, be blameworthy? Know, then, that knowledge is not blamed in itself; it is blamed only with respect to servants, for one of three reasons.

The first: that it leads to some harm, either to its possessor or to someone else, as the knowledge of sorcery and talismans is blamed. It is real, since the Qur'an bears witness to it, and that it is a means by which separation between spouses is reached. The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) was bewitched (١) and fell ill because of it until Jibril (peace be upon him) informed him of that, and the sorcery was brought out from beneath a stone at the bottom of a well. It is a kind that is derived from the knowledge of the properties of substances and of computational matters in the risings of the stars. From those substances a figure is made in the form of the bewitched person, and a specific time of the risings is observed for it, and words are joined with it that are uttered, of disbelief and obscenity contrary to the Law, and by means of them recourse is had to seeking the help of the devils. From the whole of that, by the course of Allah Most High's custom, strange conditions arise in the bewitched person. Knowing these causes, as knowledge, is not blameworthy, but it serves only to harm creation, and a means to evil is evil; so that is the reason it is blameworthy knowledge. Indeed, if someone pursues one of the friends of Allah in order to kill him, when that one has hidden from him in a secure place, then when the wrongdoer asks about his location, it is not permitted to alert him to it; rather, lying about it is obligatory, whereas mentioning his location would be guidance and imparting knowledge of the thing as it is, but it is blameworthy because it leads to harm.

The second: that it is harmful to its possessor in most cases, like the knowledge of the stars. In itself it is not blameworthy in its essence, for it is of two kinds: a computational kind, and the Qur'an has spoken to the effect that the course of the sun and the moon is reckoned, when Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said, ⟦QS 55:5⟧ and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said, ⟦QS 36:39⟧; and the second is judgments, and its sum comes back to inferring events from causes. It resembles a physician's inference from the pulse about the illness that will occur. It is knowledge of the courses of the custom of Allah Most High and His habit with His creation. But the Law has blamed it.
He (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "When destiny is mentioned, hold back; when the stars are mentioned, hold back; and when my Companions are mentioned, hold back." (٢)
And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "I fear three things for my community after me: the injustice of leaders, belief in the stars, and denial of destiny." (٣)

And 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "Learn from the stars what you are guided by on land and sea, then hold back." It was forbidden only for three reasons. One of them is that it harms most of creation, for when it is cast to them that these effects occur following the course of the planets, it falls into their souls that the planets are the effective agents and that they are the managing gods, because they are noble heavenly substances and their impact is great in hearts. So the heart remains turned toward them and sees good and evil as something to be feared or hoped for from their direction.

And the remembrance of Allah, glorified is He, is effaced from the heart. For the weak one confines his view to intermediaries, whereas the firmly grounded scholar is the one who comes to know that the sun, the moon, and the stars are made subservient by His command, glorified and exalted is He. The example of the weak person's looking to the arrival of the light of the sun following sunrise is the example of an ant, if it were given a mind, on the surface of a sheet of paper, watching the blackness of the line appear anew, and believing that it is the act of the pen, not rising in its view to witnessing the fingers, then from them to the hand, then from it to the will that moves the hand, then from it to the capable, willing writer, then from him to the Creator of the hand, the power, and the will. Thus most of the creatures' view is confined to the near, lowly causes, cut off from ascending to the Causer of causes. This is one of the reasons for the prohibition regarding the stars.

The second of them is that the judgments of the stars are pure conjecture, not grasped in the case of individual persons, neither as certainty nor as probable belief. So judging by it is judging by what is unknown, and its blame on this account is as ignorance, not as knowledge. It was a miracle of Idris (peace be upon him), as is related, but that knowledge has been effaced and obliterated. And what happens, rarely, of the astrologer being right is coincidence, because he may learn of some of the causes, but the effect does not occur following them except after many conditions whose realities it is not within human power to learn. If it happens that Allah Most High decrees the remaining causes, accuracy occurs; and if He does not decree them, he errs. That is like a person's guess that the sky will rain today whenever he sees clouds gathering and rising from the mountains, so his opinion is moved by that; yet perhaps the day grows hot with the sun and the clouds go away, or perhaps it is the opposite. Mere clouds are not sufficient for the coming of rain, and the remaining causes are not known. Likewise a sailor's guess that the ship will be safe, relying on what he is accustomed to of the habit of the winds, while those winds have hidden causes of which he is not informed, so at times he is right in his guess and at times wrong. For this reason, speech about the stars is also prevented.

The third of them is that there is no benefit in it. At the least, it is plunging into superfluities that do not avail, and wasting life, which is a person's most precious merchandise, on what is without benefit, and that is the utmost loss. The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) passed by a man around whom people had gathered, and said, "What is this?" They said, "A very learned man." He said, "In what?" They said, "In poetry and the genealogies of the Arabs." He said, "A knowledge that does not benefit and an ignorance that does not harm." (١) And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "Knowledge is only a firm verse, an established Sunna, or an equitable obligation." So then plunging into the stars and what resembles it is rushing into danger and plunging into ignorance without benefit, for what is decreed will be, and guarding against it is not possible. This is unlike medicine, for the need for it is pressing and most of its evidence is of what one can come to know; and unlike dream interpretation, although it is conjecture, because it is one of forty-six parts of prophecy and there is no danger in it.

The third reason is plunging into a knowledge from which the one who plunges in does not gain the benefit of knowledge, so it is blameworthy in his case, like learning the subtle sciences before the evident ones and the obscure before the clear, and like searching into the divine secrets, since the philosophers and the theologians look up to them but have not managed them on their own, and none has managed them on his own, nor to stand on the ways to some of them, except the prophets and the friends of Allah (awliya'). So people must be restrained from investigating them and returned to what the Law has spoken; in that is sufficiency for the one granted success. How many a person has plunged into the sciences and been harmed by them, and had he not plunged into them, his state in religion would have been better than what he came to. It is not denied that knowledge can be harmful to some people, as the flesh of birds and kinds of delicate sweets harm a suckling infant. Indeed, many a person is benefited by ignorance of some matters. It is related that someone complained to a physician of the barrenness of his wife, that she did not bear children; the physician felt her pulse and said, "You have no need of medicine for childbirth, for you will die within

forty days, and the pulse indicated it. The woman felt great fear, her life became embittered for her, she brought out her wealth and distributed it, made her will, and stayed without eating or drinking until the period elapsed and she did not die. Her husband came to the physician and said to him, "She has not died." The physician said, "I knew that. Have intercourse with her now, for she will bear." He said, "How is that?" He said, "I saw her fat, and fat had formed on the mouth of her womb, so I knew she would not become lean except through fear of death; so I frightened her with that until she became lean and the obstacle to childbirth was removed." This alerts you to sensing the danger of some sciences and makes you understand the meaning of his saying (peace and blessings be upon him), "We seek refuge in Allah from knowledge that does not benefit." (١) So take a lesson from this story and do not be a researcher into sciences that the Law has blamed and warned against. Keep to following the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) and restrict yourself to following the Sunna; for safety is in following, and danger is in investigating things and acting independently. Do not keep plunging into the depths with your opinion, your reasoning, your evidence, your proof, and your claim, "I investigate things in order to know them as they are, so what harm is there in reflecting on knowledge?" For what returns to you of its harm is greater. How many a thing you come to know, and your knowing it harms you with a harm that would almost destroy you in the Hereafter, unless Allah comes to your aid with His mercy.

Know that just as the skilled physician comes to know secrets in treatments that someone who does not know them finds improbable, so too the prophets are the physicians of hearts and those knowledgeable of the causes of the life of the Hereafter. So do not impose your reasoning upon their ways, lest you perish. How many a person suffers an affliction in his finger, and his reason dictates that he smear it, until the skilled physician alerts him that its treatment is to smear the palm on the other side of the body; and he finds that exceedingly improbable, because he does not know how the nerves branch, where they originate, and how they wind around the body. So too is the matter on the path of the Hereafter: in the fine points of the practices (sunan) of the Law and its proper conduct (adab), and in its creeds by which people have been enjoined to worship, there are secrets and subtleties that it is not within the capacity and power of reason to encompass, just as in the properties of stones there are wondrous things whose knowledge is hidden from the people of the craft, so that no one has been able to know the cause by which the magnet attracts iron. The wonders and marvels in creeds and acts, and their benefit for the clarity of hearts, their cleanness, their purity, their purification, and their being set right for ascending to the neighbourhood of Allah Most High and being exposed to the breaths of His bounty, are more and greater than what is in medicines and drugs. Just as minds fall short of grasping the benefits of medicines even though experiment is a way to them, so minds fall short of grasping what benefits in the life of the Hereafter, whereas experiment cannot reach it. Experiment could reach it only if some of the dead returned to us and told us of the accepted, beneficial acts that bring one near to Allah Most High in closeness, and of the acts that distance from Him, and likewise of the creeds; and that is something for which there is no hope. So it suffices you of the benefit of reason that it guides you to the truthfulness of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and makes you understand the sources of his indications. Then remove reason from acting, and hold fast to following, for you will not be safe except through it, and that is all. For that reason he (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "Some knowledge is ignorance, and some speech is incapacity." (٢) It is known that knowledge is not ignorance, but it has the effect of ignorance in causing harm. He (peace and blessings be upon him) also said, "A little success is better than much knowledge." (٣) And Jesus (peace be upon him) said, "How many trees there are, and not all of them bear fruit, and not all are good; and how many sciences there are, and not all of them are beneficial."
Chapter Four: On the reason for people's turning to the knowledge of disagreement (khilaf), the details of the afflictions of disputation and debate, and the conditions for permitting them

Know that the caliphate after the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) was taken up by the rightly guided, rightly directed caliphs, and they were leaders, knowers of Allah Most High, jurists in His rulings, and they were independent in issuing legal opinions in judgments, so they did not seek help from the jurists except rarely, in cases in which consultation could not be dispensed with. So the scholars were free for the knowledge of the Hereafter and devoted themselves to it, and they would pass legal opinions off from one to another, and whatever pertained to the rulings of creation concerning this world, and they turned to Allah Most High with the utmost of their striving, as is transmitted of their biographies. Then when the caliphate after them passed to people who took it up

without entitlement and without independence in the knowledge of legal opinions and rulings, they were compelled to seek help from the jurists and to keep them in company in all their circumstances in order to ask their legal opinion on the course of their rulings. There remained among the scholars of the Followers some who continued in the first pattern, adhering to the purity of religion and persisting in the way of the scholars of the early generations; when they were sought they fled and turned away. So the caliphs were compelled to insist on seeking them to assign them judgeship and governance posts. The people of those times saw the honour of the scholars and the turning of the leaders and governors toward them despite the scholars' turning away from them, so they craned their necks toward seeking knowledge as a means to obtaining honour and attaining status from the governors. They threw themselves into the knowledge of legal opinions, presented themselves to the governors, made themselves known to them, and sought posts and gifts from them. Some were deprived, some succeeded; and the successful one was not free of the humiliation of seeking and the degradation of abasement. So the jurists, after having been sought, became seekers, and after having been honoured through turning away from the sultans, became humbled by turning toward them, except those whom Allah Most High granted success in every age among the scholars of Allah's religion. The greatest turning in those times was to the knowledge of legal opinions and judgments, because of the great need for them in offices and governance. Then after them there appeared among the notables and emirs one who listened to people's statements on the foundations of creeds and whose soul inclined to hearing the arguments about them, so his desire for debate and dispute in theology (kalam) became known; and people threw themselves into theology (kalam), wrote many works in it, arranged the methods of disputations in it, and extracted the arts of contradiction in doctrines. They claimed that their aim was defending the religion of Allah, fighting for the Sunna, and suppressing the innovators, just as those before them claimed that their aim in occupying themselves with legal opinions was religion and assuming the rulings of the Muslims, out of compassion for Allah's creation and sincere counsel to them.

Then after that there appeared among the notables one who did not consider it right to plunge into theology (kalam) and open the door of disputation in it, because of the gross partisanships and widespread quarrels that had arisen from opening its door, leading to the shedding of blood and the ruin of lands. His soul inclined to disputation in jurisprudence and to clarifying which is the more fitting of the schools of ash-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with them both) in particular. So people abandoned theology and the arts of knowledge and flocked to the points of disagreement between ash-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa in particular, and were lax regarding disagreement with Malik, Sufyan, Ahmad (may Allah Most High have mercy on them), and others. They claimed that their aim was deriving the subtleties of the Law, establishing the reasons of the school, and laying the groundwork of the principles of legal opinions. They wrote many works and derivations in it and arranged kinds of disputations and compilations in it, and they continue on it to this day. We do not know what Allah will bring about in the ages after us. This is the motive for devoting oneself to disputed questions and disputations, nothing else. Had the souls of the masters of this world inclined to disagreement with another imam of the imams or to another of the sciences, they too would have inclined along with them, and would not have ceased to give the pretext that what they are occupied with is the knowledge of religion and that they have no aim except drawing near to the Lord of the worlds.
